missions.title: A definition is not a call

lesson.heading: Sound the ready signal
lesson.text: Before opening the archive door, the base-camp console announces that it is ready. The signal belongs between the startup and finish messages. Defining the signal tells Python what it does; the expedition still needs to trigger it.

lesson.heading: Predict before running
lesson.text: A `def` statement creates a function. Its indented body is saved for later; it does not run just because Python reaches the definition. A call uses parentheses to ask the function to run.
lesson.code:
def test_beacon():
    print("Beacon lit")

print("Before")
test_beacon()
print("After")

lesson.heading: Follow the detour
lesson.text: At `test_beacon()`, execution enters the function, prints its message, then returns to the next line after the call. Predict the starter output before running it. Add only the missing call; this first mission is about reading the route through the code.

missions.brief: Call `announce_ready` between the two existing outer print statements.
requirements: Call `announce_ready` between the two existing outer print statements.
Keep the function and the existing printed messages unchanged. The three lines should appear in the order shown.
missions.starter:
def announce_ready():
    print("Workshop ready")

print("Starting")
# Call the function here.
print("Finished")
hints: Which indented line never gets visited when you run the starter?
Put the call where you want the function output to appear, at the same indentation as the outer prints.
Use the function name followed by empty parentheses. You are calling it, not defining it again.

tests.label: The call happens between Starting and Finished
tests.hint: Trace the calls and the resulting output in order.

tests.label: announce_ready()
tests.hint: Check the function name, supplied arguments, returned value, and whether it should print anything.

reference.code:
def announce_ready():
    print("Workshop ready")

print("Starting")
announce_ready()
print("Finished")
notes: The definition stores the behavior; the later call runs it. Moving the call changes when its output appears.
Writing `announce_ready` without parentheses would refer to the function but would not execute its body.

missions.title: Package a repeated action
missions.concepts: Define a function · call it twice

lesson.heading: Reuse the tool prompt
lesson.text: At the equipment rack, the cartographer sees the same prompt whenever they can pick another tool. Give the prompt one home so both callers get the same wording.

lesson.heading: Give an action a name
lesson.text: A function can group an action you want to repeat. Start with `def`, a descriptive name, parentheses, and a colon. Its body is indented four spaces.

lesson.heading: One definition, several calls
lesson.text: Define the behavior once, then call it wherever needed. Repeating a function call is fine. Repeating its whole body makes later changes harder to keep consistent.

missions.title: One function, different values

lesson.heading: Greet the next cartographer
lesson.text: The console welcomes whoever signs in for the next watch. Give the greeting a name to use on each call so it works just as well for the second cartographer as the first.

lesson.heading: A parameter is a local name
lesson.text: A parameter appears inside the definition parentheses. Each call supplies an argument: the actual value the parameter will refer to during that call.

lesson.heading: Read the contract
lesson.text: For this exercise the checks call your function themselves with different names. You do not need `input()`. Keep the sample calls for Run; those calls alone are not proof the function works for other values.

greet("Morgan") prints Hello, Morgan!

missions.title: The caller can use another name

lesson.heading: Mark the selected gear
lesson.text: The desk can call the thing it picked “selected equipment” while the label printer calls it a device. What matters is the value passed across the boundary. If the desk switches gear, the printed label should switch too.

lesson.heading: Names do not need to match
lesson.text: An argument can be a variable with a completely different name. Python evaluates that argument and binds the resulting value to the parameter.
lesson.code:
def show_project(title):
    print(f"Project: {title}")

current_project = "Archive map"
show_project(current_project)

lesson.heading: Find the boundary
lesson.text: Read your calls from outside inward: what value does this outside variable hold, and which parameter receives it? The function should use its parameter rather than reaching back to an outside variable.

label_device("Radio") prints Device: Radio

missions.title: Two arguments, two jobs

lesson.heading: Put the gear where it belongs
lesson.text: The cartographer labels equipment at base camp so a teammate can find it after dark. Putting the shelf name where the equipment name belongs gives a perfectly formatted label that sends them to the wrong place.

lesson.heading: Position establishes the match
lesson.text: With ordinary positional arguments, the first value goes to the first parameter, the second to the second. Meaningful parameter names help you remember the order.

lesson.heading: Trace before fixing
lesson.text: In the starter, the function is correct but the sample call swaps two values. Work out which value each parameter currently receives, then fix only the call.

item_name = "Radio"

notes: The parameter order is part of the function contract. Swapping valid strings produces no exception, but changes the meaning.

lesson.text: The copying desk receives the name of a job and the number of sheets needed. One helper should announce both the map for a solo scout and a larger batch for a whole expedition.

missions.title: Give a value back

lesson.heading: Hand the time to the planner
lesson.text: The route planner needs a number it can compare with remaining torchlight. A number printed on screen is useful to a person, but a number returned by the helper is usable by the planner.

lesson.heading: A returned value belongs to the caller
lesson.text: `print` sends text to the output panel. `return` hands a value back to the calling expression. The caller can then print it, store it, or calculate with it.
lesson.code:
def double(value):
    return value * 2

answer = double(6)
print(answer)

lesson.heading: Checks can inspect the result
lesson.text: From here, many checks call a function and compare its return value. Printing the right number inside the function is not enough. Do not print inside the calculation function; the sample caller will handle display.

missions.title: It printed correctly. What came back?

lesson.heading: Fix the reading that never arrives
lesson.text: A helper prints the total time for a survey and its setup, yet the caller receives nothing it can put in the schedule. Watch for the difference between seeing a number and receiving it.

lesson.heading: Two different channels
lesson.text: A function can display a number and still return no useful value. If it reaches its end without `return`, the returned value is `None`, representing the absence of a value.
lesson.code:
def broken_double(value):
    print(value * 2)

answer = broken_double(4)
print(answer)
# Output: 8, then None

lesson.heading: Repair the boundary
lesson.text: Run the starter and inspect both lines. The internal calculation is right; the caller is receiving the wrong thing. Change how the function delivers its result.

lesson.heading: A call is an expression
lesson.text: A function call can appear on the right side of an assignment. The returned value, not the function, becomes the value of that variable.

def square(number):

area = square(4)
print(area)
print(area + 2)

lesson.heading: Same call, different location
lesson.text: Putting a call in an f-string does not change parameter matching or return behavior. The call must still include its arguments. This is the pattern you used in the demo project.

missions.title: Give an intermediate result a name

lesson.heading: Show the quote in stages
lesson.text: A buyer wants to see what the expedition costs before packing and verify that repeated printing gives the same packed cost. Name the stages so another cartographer can follow what changed between them.

lesson.heading: A name can explain an expression
lesson.text: A long expression can be correct yet difficult to follow. A meaningful intermediate variable gives its result a name and makes reuse straightforward.

lesson.heading: Preserve behavior while changing structure
lesson.text: Refactoring changes the organization without changing the intended behavior. The starter contains working helpers but repeats a nested expression. Replace that repetition with two named steps. Add the missing final line using the second value.

missions.brief: Read unit price and quantity as whole numbers. Keep both helper functions unchanged.
requirements: Read unit price and quantity as whole numbers. Keep both helper functions unchanged.
Set `base_cost` to the result of `batch_cost`. Set `packed_cost` to `add_packing(base_cost)`.
Print Base: VALUE, Packed: VALUE, and Packed again: VALUE in that order. Reuse `packed_cost` for both packed messages.

def batch_cost(price, quantity):
    return price * quantity

def add_packing(cost):
    return cost + 5

price = int(input())
quantity = int(input())
print(f"Packed: {add_packing(batch_cost(price, quantity))}")
print(f"Packed again: {add_packing(batch_cost(price, quantity))}")

Input: 4, then 3
Output:
Base: 12
Packed: 17
Packed again: 17
hints: Calculate the base first, then pass that value to `add_packing`.
Use the variable names requested in the contract so each stage is visible.
Once `packed_cost` exists, both packed messages can use the same variable.

tests.hint: Trace the calls and the resulting output in order.

tests.label: Another order
tests.hint: Trace the calls and the resulting output in order.

reference.code:
def batch_cost(price, quantity):
    return price * quantity

def add_packing(cost):
    return cost + 5

price = int(input())
quantity = int(input())
base_cost = batch_cost(price, quantity)
packed_cost = add_packing(base_cost)
print(f"Base: {base_cost}")
print(f"Packed: {packed_cost}")
print(f"Packed again: {packed_cost}")
notes: `base_cost` and `packed_cost` explain two distinct stages. The repeated packed value no longer requires another nested call.
The gain here is readability and avoiding unnecessary repeated work. The shorter inline form from the previous mission remains appropriate for simple one-use expressions.

missions.title: A function is not its answer

lesson.heading: Reserve time for a breather
lesson.text: Before the crew enters the archive, the planner adds a short break to the survey estimate. It needs the estimate itself, not the helper that could calculate it when called.

lesson.heading: Two valid assignments, different meanings
lesson.text: A function is itself a value. Assigning its name to another variable is legal, but it does not run the function. Assigning a call stores what the function returns.
lesson.code:
def double(value):
    return value * 2

operation = double
answer = double(6)

lesson.heading: Why the starter fails
lesson.text: The starter tries to add 5 to a function object. That is not the number it intended to calculate. Repair the assignment rather than changing the arithmetic or the helper.

lesson.text: Functions compose when one function supplies a value that another can use. Read nested calls from the inside out, or name the intermediate result.

lesson.text: The supplied helpers calculate work time and then add a `break`. The new function should connect them and return the final value. It should not print or ask for input.

missions.title: Make the arguments explicit

lesson.heading: Label gear without guessing
lesson.text: A gear label has two text fields, and both a device and a place can be called “Beacon.” Name the fields at the call site so somebody reading the call can tell which value goes where.

lesson.heading: Name the destination parameter
lesson.text: Keyword arguments use `parameter=value` in a call. Their order can differ from the definition because the names make the mapping explicit.

lesson.heading: Names belong to the definition
lesson.text: The keyword on the left must match a parameter name. The value on the right may come from any expression or outside variable. Positional arguments must come before keyword arguments if you mix the two styles.

missions.title: A useful default, not a hidden assumption

lesson.heading: Allow a longer setup
lesson.text: Most survey trips need five minutes to set up. A crew that is already packed can use zero, and an unfamiliar route might need longer. Give the common case a default and let callers supply a different value.

lesson.heading: Let a caller omit one value
lesson.text: A default in the definition is used when the caller leaves out that argument. Required parameters come before parameters with defaults.
lesson.code:
def add_margin(value, margin=2):
    return value + margin

print(add_margin(8))
print(add_margin(8, margin=5))

lesson.heading: Omitted is different from zero
lesson.text: If a caller explicitly supplies zero, Python uses zero rather than the default. A default is not a substitute for every false-looking value. We are using a simple numeric default; mutable defaults are a later topic.

missions.brief: Define `with_setup(work_minutes, setup_minutes=5)` to return their sum.
requirements: Define `with_setup(work_minutes, setup_minutes=5)` to return their sum.
Support omitted setup, a positional setup value, and a keyword setup value. Explicit zero means no setup time.
Do not print or read input inside the function.
missions.starter:
def with_setup(work_minutes, setup_minutes=5):
    pass

print(with_setup(30))
print(with_setup(30, setup_minutes=0))
missions.example:
with_setup(30) returns 35
with_setup(30, 8) returns 38

missions.title: Build a session calculation toolkit

lesson.heading: Assemble the planning desk
lesson.text: The grimoire’s first toolkit should work for any cartographer at the desk. Separate the survey time, setup time, and display label so each part can be checked or reused independently.

lesson.heading: Small contracts, one application
lesson.text: Build three reusable functions, then a short console caller that combines them. You have already practiced every operation: multiplication, adding a default amount, cleaning text, and returning a formatted string.

lesson.heading: Keep input at the edge
lesson.text: The functions receive values and return values. Only the outer program reads input and prints. That separation means the same helpers could later be used by a GUI or another program.

lesson.heading: Build and test one layer at a time
lesson.text: Start with the work-total function, then the setup function, then the formatter. Finally connect them to input. Checks call each helper independently and also run the whole program. Numeric inputs are nonnegative integers; handling invalid text and negative values is deliberately outside this project.

reference.code:
def work_minutes(length, count):
    return length * count

def with_setup(minutes, setup=5):
    return minutes + setup

def format_plan(name, minutes):
    clean_name = name.strip()
    if clean_name == "":
        clean_name = "Learner"
    return f"{clean_name}: {minutes} minutes."

name = input()
length = int(input())
count = int(input())
work = work_minutes(length, count)
planned = with_setup(work)
message = format_plan(name, planned)
print(message)
notes: Each helper has a small contract that can be checked independently. Input conversion and display stay in the outer program.
Named intermediate results make the path easy to explain and debug. A shorter nested expression would also work, but is not automatically better.
This is a reusable first version, not a production scheduler. Validation, files, and interfaces can be added later without mixing those responsibilities into the calculations.
